title: Firefighter injured at shooting scene; She's off the job after her hand was hurt while helping man shot by police at store
article: A firefighter remains off the job after injuring her hand while tending to a man who was shot and killed by police during a Kitchener robbery earlier this month.

Trevor Colin Graham, 26, a troubled man with a history of drug addiction and depression, died of a gunshot wound to the chest Nov. 20 while fleeing a Shoppers Drug Mart store with stolen prescription medication.

Fire Chief Tim Beckett said the Kitchener firefighter accidentally injured her hand while giving Graham medical treatment after the shooting in a vestibule at the front of the Sunrise Centre store on Ottawa Street South.
She was taken to the hospital, treated and released later that night but is still off work while receiving Workers' Compensation benefits.
"With an injury to the hand, she can't perform her functions as a firefighter right now," said Beckett.

He declined to discuss the nature of the injury or whether it was caused by a weapon such as a knife. Beckett also wouldn't say if there are any heightened concerns the firefighter may be at risk of contracting a communicable disease because of her injury.
"Anybody working on the patient could have been exposed to body fluids, particularly blood," he said. "We look at all of our staff and ensure everybody is looked after."
The shooting death is being investigated by the Special Investigations Unit, a civilian agency that looks into all police incidents involving death or serious injury.
The agency has not said if Graham was armed or what led to the shooting after two uniformed officers responding to a robbery call confronted him as he was leaving the store.
Graham had an armed confrontation with OPP officers at his home in Paris, Ont., this summer.

He threatened officers with a knife and at one point, according to a police report, yelled at them to shoot him in the head. His mother has said Graham was doing well in a methadone treatment program after being addicted for years to a prescription painkiller called OxyContin.
Frank Phillips, a spokesperson for the civilian agency, said it's not known how long the probe into possible police wrongdoing will take.
